title: AQA GCSE Physics · Forces and Elasticity

items.stem: Which statement describes a scalar quantity?

options.text: It is described by a magnitude only, and never by a direction.
It is described by a magnitude and also by a direction.
It is a quantity that does not describe anything moving.
It is described by an arrow that can be any length.

items.why: Scalar quantities have magnitude only, which is exactly what this states.

items.stem: Which statement is true of a vector quantity but not of a scalar quantity?

options.text: It can be given a size in a unit such as the newton.
It always describes an object that is moving.
It can be shown as a label on a scale diagram.
It has a direction associated with its magnitude.

items.why: Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction, and that direction is what a scalar lacks.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what a force is?

options.text: A property of an object that heavy objects have more of.
Something stored in a moving object and used up later.
A push or pull that acts only when two objects touch.
A push or pull on an object due to another object.

items.why: A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of a contact force?

options.text: The tension in a stretched tow-rope
The magnetic force between two bar magnets
The gravitational force on a falling ball
The electrostatic force between charges

items.why: Tension is listed by the specification as a contact force, alongside friction and air resistance.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of a non-contact force?

options.text: The air resistance on a falling skydiver
The upthrust on a boat floating on the sea.
The drag on a fish swimming in the water.
The electrostatic force between charges

items.why: Electrostatic force is listed by the specification as a non-contact force.

items.stem: Which pair of forces are both non-contact forces?

options.text: Magnetic and gravitational forces
Air resistance and electrostatic force
Drag in water and the magnetic force.
Upthrust and a gravitational force.

items.why: Both are listed by the specification as non-contact forces, acting between separated objects.

items.stem: Which statement about the weight of a book resting on a shelf is correct?

options.text: It is the total amount of matter contained in the book.
It is the push of the shelf upwards on the book.
It is a property the book has whatever happens.
It is the force acting on the book due to gravity.

items.why: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity, which close to the Earth is due to its gravitational field.

items.stem: Which equation is used to calculate the weight of an object?

options.text: weight = mass ÷ the gravitational field strength
weight = mass plus gravitational field strength
mass = weight × gravitational field strength g
weight = mass × gravitational field strength

items.why: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it, W = m g.

items.stem: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = m g?

options.text: W in newtons, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
W in kilograms, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
W in grams, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
W in newtons, m in kilograms and g in newtons of force

items.why: These are the units exactly as the specification gives them: N, kg and N/kg.

items.stem: What does g stand for in the equation W = m g, and what is its unit?

options.text: Gravitational field strength, measured in newtons per kilogram
The force of gravity acting on the object, given in newtons
The weight of the object, measured in kilograms.
The strength of gravity there, measured in kilograms

items.why: The specification gives gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.

items.stem: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional. What does this mean?

options.text: Weight increases by a fixed amount each time mass increases.
Doubling the mass doubles the weight in the same field.
Weight just gets bigger by some amount when mass increases.
Weight and mass are equal when the units are ignored.

items.why: Directly proportional means one quantity is a fixed multiple of the other, so the factor carries across.

items.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the weight of an object?

options.text: A set of kitchen scales marked in kilograms
An electronic balance reading in kilograms
A spring-balance calibrated in newtons
A balance comparing two known masses

items.why: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance, also called a newtonmeter.

items.stem: What is meant by the resultant force on an object?

options.text: The largest of all of the forces that are acting on the object.
The force that is left once the object has stopped moving.
The single force with the same effect as all of them together.
The total of the sizes of every force that acts on it.

items.why: A number of forces may be replaced by a single force with the same effect: the resultant force.

items.stem: A single force is resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The two components together have the same effect as the force.
The two components add up numerically to the size of the single force.
Each component is exactly half the size of the original single force.
The two components replace a force that has no direction.

items.why: The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.

items.stem: Two forces are drawn as arrows on the same diagram. One arrow is twice as long as the other. What does this tell you?

options.text: The two forces are equal, but drawn at two different scales.
The longer arrow was drawn bigger just to look neat.
The force shown by the longer arrow is twice as large.
Arrow length is up to the artist and shows nothing.

items.why: The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, so a doubled length is a doubled force.

items.stem: A crate is dragged across a rough floor. Why is the friction between the crate and the floor a contact force?

options.text: Because the crate stays right next to the floor below.
Because the crate is also touching the air around it.
Because the crate and the floor are physically touching.
Because the crate rests on the ground, not falling.

items.why: Contact forces are those where the objects are physically touching, which the crate and floor are.

items.stem: The Earth pulls on a satellite high above its surface. Why is this gravitational force a non-contact force?

options.text: Because there is no air in space to pass the force along.
Because the Earth and the satellite are physically separated.
Because the two objects can never touch one another.
Because the satellite's mass and weight are lower in space.

items.why: Non-contact forces act between objects that are physically separated, which is the case here.

items.stem: A student writes that the force on a trolley is 12 N. Why is this description incomplete?

options.text: Because the mass in kilograms was not given too.
Because force is a vector, so a direction is needed.
Because a force in newtons must be converted to kilograms.
Because a vector must also be given a speed.

items.why: Force is a vector quantity, so a full description gives the magnitude and the direction.

items.stem: A tennis ball is struck by a racket. Which statement describes the interaction between them correctly?

options.text: Only the racket exerts a force, because it moved first of all.
The racket pushes the ball harder than the ball pushes the racket.
Each exerts a force on the other, equal in size and opposite in direction.
Both forces act on the ball, so they cancel and it cannot move.

items.why: The two objects interact, and the interaction produces a force on each of them, drawn as a pair of vectors.

items.stem: An astronaut takes a 3 kg toolbox from the Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). What happens?

options.text: Its mass and weight both fall, because gravity is weaker there.
Its mass and weight both drop to about a sixth.
Its mass stays at 3 kg but its weight becomes smaller.
Its mass and its weight do not change on the way there.

items.why: Mass does not depend on location; weight depends on the gravitational field strength at that point.

items.stem: A rock has a mass of 12 kg. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the weight of the rock?
items.why: W = m g = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N, with weight in newtons.

items.stem: A bag has a weight of 49 N at a place where the gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the mass of the bag?

options.text: 5 kg
0.2 kg

items.why: Rearranging W = m g gives m = W ÷ g = 49 ÷ 9.8 = 5 kg.

items.stem: Why is the weight of an object drawn as a single arrow from one point on it?

options.text: Because weight acts where the object presses on the surface below.
Because the weight may be taken to act at the centre of mass.
Because gravity only acts on the part touching the ground.
Because a vector must always be drawn from the ground.

items.why: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point, its centre of mass.

items.stem: A box is pulled to the right with a force of 12 N while a friction force of 5 N acts to the left. What is the resultant force?

options.text: 17 N, acting to the right
12 N acting to the right
7 N acting to the left
7 N acting to the right

items.why: For forces in a straight line the resultant is 12 - 5 = 7 N, in the direction of the larger force.

items.stem: A ball hangs at rest on the end of a string. A free body diagram of the ball is drawn. Which forces should appear on it?

options.text: The tension in the string and the pull of the ball on the string as well.
The weight of the ball and the pull of the ball on the Earth below.
The weight of the ball and the tension in the string, both acting on the ball.
No forces at all, because the ball is hanging still on the string.

items.why: A free body diagram shows the isolated object with only the forces that act on it.

items.stem: Two forces at right angles act on a point. A student draws them to scale, head to tail, to find the resultant. What must the final answer state?

options.text: The magnitude in newtons only, since that is the number asked for.
The magnitude in newtons and the direction of the force.
The direction only, because a scale drawing cannot give a size.
The magnitude in newtons and the total length of both arrows.

items.why: The resultant is a vector, so the answer gives both magnitude and direction from the scale drawing.

items.stem: A block of mass 4 kg has a weight of 24 N on a planet. A second block on the same planet has a mass of 12 kg. What is its weight?

options.text: 32 N, because the extra 8 kg of mass adds another 8 N to the weight.
72 N, because the mass is three times larger and so the weight is too.
2 N, because the mass is divided by the gravitational field strength.
36 N, because the weight goes up by 12 N for each extra block.

items.why: Weight and mass are directly proportional, so a mass three times larger gives a weight three times larger.

items.stem: A parachutist falls at a steady speed. Her weight is 700 N. What can be said about the forces on her?

options.text: The forces cancel out, so really no force acts at all.
Air resistance is 700 N upwards, so the resultant force is zero.
Her weight and the air resistance are an action pair.
No forces act on her now, since her speed is not changing.

items.why: The forces are balanced: an upward 700 N air resistance and a 700 N weight give a resultant of zero.

items.stem: Which statement describes elastic deformation?

options.text: The object keeps part of its extra length after the forces are removed.
The object is made of rubber, so it stretches much further than metal does.
The object breaks into pieces as soon as the stretching force is removed.
The object returns to its original shape once the forces are removed.

items.why: Elastic deformation is defined by full recovery of the original shape when the forces are removed.

items.stem: A spring is loaded with weights, staying below its limit of proportionality. Which statement about the force and the extension is correct?

options.text: The extension is directly proportional to the total length of the spring used.
The force is proportional to the extension whatever the load size.
The extension is directly proportional to the force applied to the spring.
The extension is proportional to the spring constant of that spring.

items.why: This is the specification statement: extension is directly proportional to force below the limit of proportionality.

items.stem: What does the limit of proportionality of a spring tell you?

options.text: The force at which the spring finally snaps and can carry no more load.
The force beyond which the spring will not return to its original length.
The largest length the spring reaches before it stops stretching.
The largest force for which extension stays proportional to force.

items.why: Up to this force the graph is a straight line through the origin; beyond it, proportionality is lost.

items.stem: Which statement about the quantities in the equation F = k e is correct?

options.text: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons, N, as a force is.
The extension, e, is measured in centimetres, cm, in this equation.
The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons per metre, written N/m.
The extension, e, is the whole length of the stretched spring.

items.why: F is in newtons, k is in newtons per metre and e is in metres.

items.stem: A spring is squashed rather than stretched. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A different equation is needed, because F = k e only covers stretching.
F = k e still applies, with e as the compression of the spring.
No energy is stored, because energy is only stored by stretching a spring.
The spring constant becomes negative when the spring is compressed.

items.why: The specification states that the relationship also applies to compression, with e as the compression.

items.stem: A spring is stretched by a force and is not inelastically deformed. How does the elastic potential energy stored compare with the work done on the spring?

options.text: The energy stored is slightly less, because some energy is wasted.
The energy stored is much smaller, because a lot of energy is wasted.
No work is done at all, because the spring stays in one place.
The energy stored is equal to the work done on the spring by the force.

items.why: The specification states that the work done and the elastic potential energy stored are equal in this case.

items.stem: A rubber band is held by a clamp at one end while a student pulls the other end, and the band stretches. Which statement describes the forces that stretch the band?

options.text: Two forces act on the band, pulling its two ends in opposite directions.
One pulling force acts on the band, along the line of the band.
Two forces act on the band, both pulling it towards the clamp.
The weight of the band is the only force acting, and it stretches it.

items.why: Deforming a stationary object needs more than one force, and to stretch it the forces must pull the ends apart.

items.stem: A car is parked on level ground and the springs in its suspension are squashed. Which pair of forces compresses one of these springs?

options.text: The weight of the car is the only force acting on the spring.
The car body pushes down on the spring and the axle pushes up on it.
The car body and the axle both push down on the spring from above it.
The spring squashes under its own weight as it hangs there.

items.why: Compression needs two forces pushing the ends of the spring towards each other.

items.stem: A steel spring is stretched by a very large force. When the force is removed the spring is longer than it was at the start. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It has been elastically deformed, because its shape changed while pulled.
It has been inelastically deformed, so it has not returned to its original shape.
It cannot have deformed elastically, since steel is not a stretchy material.
It has been inelastically deformed, so the metal has begun to break apart.

items.why: Not returning to the original length after the force is removed is exactly inelastic deformation.

items.stem: A spring has a spring constant of 120 N/m and is stretched by 25 cm, which is below its limit of proportionality. Using force = spring constant × extension, what is the force applied to the spring?
A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. What is the spring constant of this spring?

options.text: 50 N/m

items.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 2000 N/m is stretched by 8.0 cm, below its limit of proportionality. Using elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2, how much energy is stored?
A spring with a spring constant of 800 N/m is compressed by 3.0 cm and then released, pushing a trolley along a smooth bench. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?

options.text: The compressed spring holds no energy, so nothing moves the trolley.
No energy is transferred, because a compressed spring stores no energy.
The elastic potential energy store of the spring empties to the kinetic store.
The energy stored is transferred to the thermal store of the bench.

items.why: Releasing the spring transfers the stored elastic potential energy to the kinetic energy store of the trolley.

items.stem: In required practical activity 6, a spring hangs from a clamp stand and weights are added one at a time. Which method gives the most reliable value for the extension?

options.text: Take the spring off the stand after each weight and measure it flat on the bench.
Read the ruler from wherever you are sitting, since a scale reading cannot change.
Record the length of the loaded spring itself and use that as the extension.
Measure the loaded length at eye level and subtract the original length.

items.why: The extension is the loaded length minus the unloaded length, and reading a vertical ruler at eye level avoids parallax error.

items.stem: Why must more than one force be applied to a stationary object in order to change its shape?

options.text: A single force on its own is enough to stretch the object into a new shape.
Forces always occur in pairs, so a second force appears without being applied.
A single force would leave a resultant force, so the object would accelerate.
One force by itself will stretch the object, so no second force is needed.

items.why: With one force there is a resultant force; the object would move off rather than deform, so a second force is needed.

items.stem: Spring A has a spring constant of 30 N/m and spring B has a spring constant of 90 N/m. The same force is applied to each spring. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Spring B extends less, because a larger spring constant means a stiffer spring.
Spring B extends more, because a larger spring constant means more stretch.
Both springs extend by exactly the same amount, because the same force is applied.
Spring B extends three times as far as spring A does under this force.

items.why: Since e = F / k, a larger spring constant gives a smaller extension for the same force.

items.stem: A spring is stretched so far that it is inelastically deformed. Which statement about the work done on the spring is correct?

options.text: The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored in it.
The work done is still exactly equal to the elastic potential energy stored.
The work done equals the energy stored, because they are always the same.
No work is done, because the spring does not spring back again.

items.why: The equality holds only when the spring is not inelastically deformed; here some work is transferred elsewhere.

items.stem: A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to 8 N, and curves above 8 N. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The curved readings are anomalies and should be left out of the graph.
The relationship is linear up to 8 N and non-linear above 8 N.
The curved part shows the spring becoming stiffer as the load increases.
The curved part is caused by measurement errors in the larger readings.

items.why: A straight line through the origin is a linear relationship; the curved region above 8 N is non-linear.

items.stem: The extension of a spring is doubled, and the spring stays below its limit of proportionality. What happens to the elastic potential energy stored in it?

options.text: It becomes four times as large, because the extension is squared.
It doubles, because the energy is proportional to the extension.
It stays the same, because the spring constant has not changed.
It doubles too, because the energy just follows the extension.

items.why: E_e = 1/2 k e^2, so multiplying e by 2 multiplies the stored energy by 4.

items.stem: In an investigation of force and extension, a student records: 1.0 N, 2.0 cm; 2.0 N, 4.0 cm; 3.0 N, 6.0 cm; 4.0 N, 8.0 cm; 5.0 N, 12.0 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: All five points fit a straight line, so k is 50 N/m for the spring.
The first four points give k = 50 N/m, and the last point is off the line.
The spring constant is 0.42 N/m, taken from the last pair of readings.
The spring became stiffer at 5.0 N, because the extension jumped by 4.0 cm.

items.why: The first four points give a constant 2.0 cm per newton, so k = 1.0 / 0.020 = 50 N/m, and the 5.0 N point does not fit.
